{{Short description|Theorem in probability theory}}

In [[probability theory]], '''Isserlis's theorem''' or '''Wick's probability theorem''' is a formula that allows one to compute higher-order moments of the [[multivariate normal distribution]] in terms of its [[covariance matrix]].  It is named after [[Leon Isserlis]].

This theorem is also particularly important in [[particle physics]], where it is known as ''[[Wick's theorem]]'' after the work of {{harvtxt|Wick|1950}}.<ref>{{cite journal
  | last = Wick
  | first = G.C.
  | year = 1950
  | title = The evaluation of the collision matrix

  | volume = 80
  | issue = 2
  | pages = 268–272
  | doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.80.268
  | bibcode = 1950PhRv...80..268W
  }}</ref> Other applications include the analysis of portfolio returns,<ref>{{cite journal
  | last1 = Repetowicz
  | first1 = Przemysław
  | last2 = Richmond
  | first2 = Peter
  | year = 2005
  | title = Statistical inference of multivariate distribution parameters for non-Gaussian distributed time series
  | journal = Acta Physica Polonica B
  | volume = 36
  | issue = 9
  | pages = 2785–2796
  | url = http://th-www.if.uj.edu.pl/acta/vol36/pdf/v36p2785.pdf
  | bibcode = 2005AcPPB..36.2785R
 }}</ref> quantum field theory<ref>{{cite journal
  | last1 = Perez-Martin
  | first1 = S.
  | last2 = Robledo
  | first2 = L.M.
  | year = 2007
  | title = Generalized Wick's theorem for multiquasiparticle overlaps as a limit of Gaudin's theorem
  | journal = Physical Review C
  | volume = 76
  | issue = 6
 | article-number = 064314
 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevC.76.064314
  | arxiv = 0707.3365
  | bibcode = 2007PhRvC..76f4314P
  | s2cid = 119627477
 }}</ref> and generation of colored noise.<ref>{{cite journal
  | last = Bartosch
  | first = L.
  | year = 2001
  | title = Generation of colored noise
  | journal = International Journal of Modern Physics C
  | volume = 12
  | issue = 6

  | doi = 10.1142/S0129183101002012
  | bibcode = 2001IJMPC..12..851B
  | s2cid = 54500670
 }}</ref>

==Statement==
If <math>(X_1,\dots, X_{n})</math> is a zero-mean [[multivariate normal]] random vector, then<math display="block">\operatorname{E} [\,X_1 X_2\cdots X_{n}\,] = \sum_{p\in P_n^2}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in p} \operatorname{E}[\,X_i X_j\,] = \sum_{p\in P_n^2}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in p}  \operatorname{Cov}(\,X_i, X_j\,), </math>where the sum is over all the pairings of <math>\{1,\ldots,n\}</math>, i.e. all distinct ways of partitioning <math>\{1,\ldots,n\}</math> into pairs <math>\{i,j\}</math>, and the product is over the pairs contained in <math>p</math>.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/gaussian-hilbert-spaces/658C87D5A0E7FB440FC34D82B08167FC|title=Gaussian Hilbert Spaces|last=Janson|first=Svante|date=June 1997|publisher=Cambridge Core|access-date=2019-11-30|doi=10.1017/CBO9780511526169|isbn=978-0-521-56128-0}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
  | last1 = Michalowicz
  | first1 = J.V.
  | last2 = Nichols
  | first2 = J.M.
  | last3 = Bucholtz
  | first3 = F.
  | last4 = Olson
  | first4 = C.C.
  | title = An Isserlis' theorem for mixed Gaussian variables: application to the auto-bispectral density
  | journal = Journal of Statistical Physics
  | year = 2009
  | volume = 136
  | issue = 1
  | pages = 89–102
  | doi = 10.1007/s10955-009-9768-3
  | bibcode = 2009JSP...136...89M
  | s2cid = 119702133
 }}</ref>

More generally, if <math>(Z_1,\dots, Z_{n})</math> is a zero-mean ''complex''-valued multivariate normal random vector, then the formula still holds.

The expression on the right-hand side is also known as the [[hafnian]] of the covariance matrix of <math>(X_1,\dots, X_{n})</math>.

=== Odd case ===
If <math>n=2m+1</math> is odd, there does not exist any pairing of <math>\{1,\ldots,2m+1\}</math>. Under this hypothesis, Isserlis's theorem implies that<math display="block">\operatorname{E}[\,X_1 X_2\cdots X_{2m+1}\,] = 0.</math>
This also follows from the fact that <math>-X=(-X_1,\dots,-X_n)</math> has the same distribution as <math>X</math>, which implies that <math>\operatorname{E}[\,X_1 \cdots X_{2m+1}\,]=\operatorname{E}[\,(-X_1) \cdots (-X_{2m+1})\,]=-\operatorname{E}[\,X_1 \cdots X_{2m+1}\,] = 0</math>.

=== Even case ===
In his original paper,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Isserlis |first=L. |year=1918 |title=On a formula for the product-moment coefficient of any order of a normal frequency distribution in any number of variables |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1431593 |journal=[[Biometrika]] |volume=12 |issue=1–2 |pages=134–139 |doi=10.1093/biomet/12.1-2.134 |jstor=2331932 |author-link=Leon Isserlis}}</ref> [[Leon Isserlis]] proves this theorem by [[mathematical induction]], generalizing the formula for the  <math>4^{\text{th}}</math> order moments,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Isserlis |first=L. |year=1916 |title=On Certain Probable Errors and Correlation Coefficients of Multiple Frequency Distributions with Skew Regression |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1431585 |journal=[[Biometrika]] |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=185–190 |doi=10.1093/biomet/11.3.185 |jstor=2331846 |author-link=Leon Isserlis}}</ref> which takes the appearance
:<math>
    \operatorname{E}[\,X_1 X_2 X_3 X_4\,] =
        \operatorname{E}[X_1X_2]\,\operatorname{E}[X_3X_4] +
        \operatorname{E}[X_1X_3]\,\operatorname{E}[X_2X_4] +
        \operatorname{E}[X_1X_4]\,\operatorname{E}[X_2X_3].
  </math>
If <math>n=2m</math> is even, there exist <math>(2m)!/(2^{m}m!) = (2m-1)!!</math> (see [[double factorial]]) pair partitions of <math>\{1,\ldots,2m\}</math>: this yields <math>(2m)!/(2^{m}m!) = (2m-1)!!</math> terms in the sum. For example, for <math>4^{\text{th}}</math> order moments (i.e. <math>4</math> random variables) there are three terms. For <math>6^{\text{th}}</math>-order moments there are <math>3\times 5=15</math> terms, and for <math>8^{\text{th}}</math>-order moments there are <math>3\times5\times7 = 105</math> terms.

=== Example ===
We can evaluate the [[Characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]] of gaussians by the Isserlis theorem:<math display="block">E[e^{-iX}] = \sum_k \frac{(-i)^k}{k!} E[X^k] = \sum_k \frac{(-i)^{2k}}{(2k)!} E[X^{2k}] = \sum_k \frac{(-i)^{2k}}{(2k)!} \frac{(2k)!}{k!2^k} E[X^{2}]^k = e^{-\frac 12 E[X^2]}</math>

== Proof ==
Since both sides of the formula are multilinear in <math> X_1, ..., X_n</math>, if we can prove the real case, we get the complex case for free.

Let <math>\Sigma_{ij} = \operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j)</math> be the covariance matrix, so that we have the zero-mean [[multivariate normal]] random vector <math>(X_1, ..., X_n) \sim N(0, \Sigma)</math>. Since both sides of the formula are continuous with respect to <math>\Sigma</math>, it suffices to prove the case when <math>\Sigma</math> is invertible. In particular, this means that if some of <math>X_1, \dots, X_n</math> are identical, such as in <math>E[X_1^3 X_2]</math>, then it reduces to the case where all variables are linearly independent, as in <math>E[X_1 X_2 X_3 X_4]</math>.

Using quadratic factorization <math>-x^T\Sigma^{-1}x/2 + v^Tx - v^T\Sigma v/2 = -(x-\Sigma v)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-\Sigma v)/2</math>, we get 

<math display="block">\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^n\det\Sigma}}\int e^{-x^T\Sigma^{-1}x/2 + v^Tx} dx = e^{v^T\Sigma v/2}</math>

[[Leibniz integral rule|Differentiate under the integral sign]] with <math>\partial_{v_1, ..., v_n}|_{v_1, ..., v_n=0}</math> to obtain<math display="block">E[X_1\cdots X_n] = \partial_{v_1, ..., v_n}\Big|_{v_1, ..., v_n=0}e^{v^T\Sigma v/2}</math>That is, we need only find the coefficient of term <math>v_1\cdots v_n</math> in the Taylor expansion of<math display="block">e^{v^T\Sigma v/2} = \sum_m \frac{1}{2^m m!} (v^T\Sigma v)^m</math>Since the quantity is even in <math>v</math>, if <math>n</math> is odd, this is zero. So let <math>n = 2m</math>, then we need only find the coefficient of term <math>v_1 v_2\cdots v_{2m-1} v_{2m}</math> in the polynomial <math>\frac{1}{2^m m!} \left(\sum_{ij}v_iv_j \Sigma_{ij}\right)^m</math>. 

Combinatorially, each pairing <math>\pi</math> of <math>1, 2, \dots, 2m-1, 2m</math> corresponds to a way to obtain <math>v_1 v_2\cdots v_{2m-1} v_{2m}</math>, by picking one <math>v_i v_j \Sigma_{ij}</math> from each bracket for each <math>(i, j) \in \pi</math>. There are <math>2^m m!</math> ways to pick in this way, cancelling out the <math>\frac{1}{2^m m!}</math> term. <math>\square</math>

== Generalizations ==

=== Gaussian integration by parts ===
An equivalent formulation of the Wick's probability formula is the Gaussian [[integration by parts]]. If <math>(X_1,\dots X_{n})</math> is a zero-mean [[multivariate normal]] random vector, then

<math display="block">\operatorname{E}(X_1 f(X_1,\ldots,X_n))=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \operatorname{Cov}(X_1, X_i)\operatorname{E}(\partial_{X_i}f(X_1,\ldots,X_n)).</math>This is a generalization of [[Stein's lemma]].

The Wick's probability formula can be recovered by induction, considering the function <math>f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}</math> defined by <math>f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=x_2\ldots x_n</math>. Among other things, this formulation is important in [[Liouville field theory|Liouville conformal field theory]] to obtain [[conformal Ward identities]], [[BPZ equations]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kupiainen|first1=Antti|last2=Rhodes|first2=Rémi|last3=Vargas|first3=Vincent|date=2019-11-01|title=Local Conformal Structure of Liouville Quantum Gravity|journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics|volume=371|issue=3|pages=1005–1069|doi=10.1007/s00220-018-3260-3|issn=1432-0916|bibcode=2019CMaPh.371.1005K|arxiv=1512.01802|s2cid=55282482}}</ref> and to prove the [[Fyodorov-Bouchaud formula]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Remy|first=Guillaume|title=The Fyodorov–Bouchaud formula and Liouville conformal field theory|journal=Duke Mathematical Journal|year=2020|volume=169|doi=10.1215/00127094-2019-0045|arxiv=1710.06897|s2cid=54777103}}</ref>

=== Non-Gaussian random variables ===
For non-Gaussian random variables, the moment-[[cumulant]]s formula<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Leonov |first1=V. P. |last2=Shiryaev |first2=A. N. |title=On a Method of Calculation of Semi-Invariants |journal=Theory of Probability & Its Applications |date=January 1959 |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=319–329 |doi=10.1137/1104031 |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/1104031|url-access=subscription }}</ref> replaces the Wick's probability formula. If <math>(X_1,\dots X_{n})</math> is a vector of [[random variable]]s, then <math display="block">\operatorname{E}(X_1 \ldots X_n)=\sum_{p\in P_n} \prod_{b\in p} \kappa\big((X_i)_{i\in b}\big),</math>where the sum is over all the [[Partition of a set|partitions]] of <math>\{1,\ldots,n\}</math>, the product is over the blocks of <math>p</math> and <math>\kappa\big((X_i)_{i\in b}\big)</math> is the [[Cumulant#Joint_cumulants|joint cumulant]] of <math>(X_i)_{i\in b}</math>.

=== Uniform distribution on the unit sphere ===
Consider <math>X = (X_1,\dots,X_d)</math> uniformly distributed on the unit sphere <math>S^{d-1}</math>, so that <math>\|X\|=1</math> [[almost surely]]. In this setting, the following holds.

If <math>n</math> is odd,
<math display="block">\operatorname{E}\bigl[X_{i_1}\,X_{i_2}\,\cdots\,X_{i_n}\bigr] \;=\; 0.\!</math>

If <math>n = 2k</math> is even,
<math display="block">\operatorname{E}\bigl[X_{i_1}\,\cdots\,X_{i_{2k}}\bigr]
\;=\;
\frac{1}{d\,\bigl(d+2\bigr)\bigl(d+4\bigr)\cdots\bigl(d + 2k - 2\bigr)}
\sum_{p \in P_{2k}^2}
  \prod_{\{r,s\}\in p} \delta_{\,i_r,i_s},</math>
where <math>P_{2k}^2</math> is the set of all pairings of <math>\{1,\ldots,2k\}</math>, <math>\delta_{i,j}</math> is the [[Kronecker delta]].

Since there are <math>|P_{2k}^2|=(2k - 1)!!</math> delta-terms, we get on the diagonal: 
<math display="block">\operatorname{E}[\,X_1^{2k}\,]
\;=\;
\frac{(2k - 1)!!}{d\,\bigl(d+2\bigr)\bigl(d+4\bigr)\cdots\bigl(d + 2k - 2\bigr)}.
</math>
Here, <math>(2k - 1)!!</math> denotes the [[double factorial]].

These results are discussed in the context of random vectors and irreducible representations in the work by Kushkuley (2021).<ref>{{cite arXiv | last=Kushkuley | first=Alexander | title=A Remark on Random Vectors and Irreducible Representations | eprint=2110.15504 | year=2021| class=math.PR }}</ref>
